quality.question: My grey text on a white background looks faint, is that a problem?
quality.answer: WCAG 2.2 Level AA, Success Criterion 1.4.3, requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for text, or 3:1 for large-scale text. [1] Exceptions include text in inactive interface components, decorative text, text not visible to anyone, text within certain pictures, and text that is part of a logo or brand name. [1]

quality.question: buttons too small?
quality.answer: For WCAG 2.2 Level AA, Success Criterion 2.5.8 requires pointer targets to be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, unless an exception applies, such as sufficient spacing around a smaller target. [5] Level AAA, Success Criterion 2.5.5, requires targets to be at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels, with its stated exceptions. [1]

quality.question: What contrast do large text and icons need?
quality.answer:
- Inactive text and text that is pure decoration, not visible, or part of a picture with significant other visual content have no contrast requirement; neither do logotypes. [3][2]
- Exceptions apply to inactive components, components whose appearance is set by the user agent and not modified by the author, and graphics presentations essential to the information conveyed. [1]

quality.question: What's the difference between 1.4.3 and 1.4.6?
quality.answer:
SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) is Level AA: text generally needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large-scale text. [1]  
SC 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) is Level AAA: text generally needs at least 7:1, or 4.5:1 for large-scale text. [2]  
Both criteria exempt inactive interface components, pure decoration, text that is not visible, certain text within pictures, and text that is part of a logo or brand name. [1][2]

quality.question: Does disabled button text need good contrast?
quality.answer: WCAG 2.2 Level AA Success Criterion 1.4.11 exempts inactive user interface components, such as disabled buttons, from contrast requirements. [1][3]

quality.question: Does a logo need to meet contrast rules?
quality.answer: Under WCAG 2.2 Level AA, text that is part of a logo or brand name has no contrast requirement under SC 1.4.3, and logos are exempt under SC 1.4.11. [5][2] However, if a logo is presented with insufficient contrast by author choice rather than brand requirements, it is not exempt under SC 1.4.11. [2]

quality.answer: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed, so it is not a current requirement. [4]

quality.question: At what width must content reflow without horizontal scrolling?
quality.answer: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.10 (Level AA), vertically scrolling content must reflow at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels without requiring two-dimensional scrolling, except for content that requires a two-dimensional layout for its usage or meaning. [1]

quality.question: How many times per second can content flash?
quality.answer: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.3.1, Level A, content must not flash more than three times in any one-second period, unless the flash is below the general flash and red flash thresholds. [3] The thresholds also allow up to three general flashes and/or three red flashes in any one-second period. [5]

quality.question: Can I use a puzzle CAPTCHA on my login page?
quality.answer: Yes, but under WCAG 2.2 Level A, Success Criterion 1.1.1, a CAPTCHA must have a text alternative that identifies and describes its purpose, and alternative CAPTCHA forms using different sensory output modes must be provided to accommodate different disabilities. [2][3] G143 is one sufficient technique for the text alternative, but it is not required; it says the alternative should identify the CAPTCHA and the task, and explain how to find an alternate version when one is available. [1][4]

quality.question: Quel est le contraste minimum pour le texte ?
quality.answer: Au niveau AA, le critère WCAG 2.2 1.4.3 exige un contraste d’au moins 4,5:1 pour le texte et les images de texte. [1][3] Pour le texte de grande taille, le minimum est de 3:1. [1][3] Des exceptions s’appliquent notamment au texte de logos, aux éléments décoratifs et aux composants d’interface inactifs, qui n’ont pas d’exigence de contraste. [1][3]
